{{Short description|Area of all the sides of the object, excluding the area of its base and top}}
[[File:Kreiszylinder.svg|thumb|440px|Straight circular cylinder with unrolled lateral surface]]
The '''lateral surface''' of a [[Three-dimensional space|three-dimensional]] object is the surface of all its sides, excluding its [[base (geometry)|base]] and top (when they exist).<ref name="Jacobs">{{citation |first=Harold R. |last=Jacobs |title=Geometry |publisher=Freeman & Co. |year=1974 |page=591 |isbn=0-7167-0456-0}}</ref> The distinction between lateral and non-lateral surfaces is most commonly applied to [[prism (geometry)|prisms]], [[cylinder (geometry)|cylinders]], [[pyramid (geometry)|pyramids]], and [[cone]]s, where there is a natural separation between the base face(s) and the remaining faces or curved surface.

==Definition==
The '''lateral surface area''' ('''LSA''') is the [[area]] of the lateral surface. This is distinguished from the '''total surface area''' ('''TSA'''), which is the lateral surface area together with the areas of the base and top.<ref name="Jacobs"/> In practical applications, the lateral surface area is relevant when calculating quantities such as the amount of material needed to wrap the sides of a container, the area of a wall to be painted, or the label for a cylindrical can.<ref name="Alexander">{{cite book |first1=Daniel C. |last1=Alexander |first2=Geralyn M. |last2=Koeberlein |title=Elementary Geometry for College Students |edition=7th |publisher=Cengage Learning |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-337-61408-5}}</ref>

==Formulas==

===Prism===
The lateral surface area of a [[prism (geometry)|prism]] is the sum of the areas of its lateral faces (the faces that are not bases).<ref name="Jacobs"/> For a '''right prism''' — one whose lateral edges are perpendicular to the bases — the lateral surface area equals the [[perimeter]] of the base multiplied by the height of the prism:<ref name="PrenticeHall">{{cite book |publisher=Prentice Hall |title=Geometry |page=700}}</ref>

:{{math|1=''A''<sub>lateral</sub> = ''P'' ⋅ ''h''}}

where {{mvar|P}} is the perimeter of the base and {{mvar|h}} is the height (the perpendicular distance between the two bases).

As a special case, for a [[cube]] with edge length {{mvar|a}}, the lateral surface area consists of four square faces: {{math|1=''A''<sub>lateral</sub> = 4''a''<sup>2</sup>}}.

For a [[rectangular prism]] (cuboid) with base dimensions {{mvar|l}} and {{mvar|w}} and height {{mvar|h}}, the lateral surface area is:

:{{math|1=''A''<sub>lateral</sub> = 2(''l'' + ''w'') ⋅ ''h''}}

===Cylinder===
[[File:Kreiszylinder.svg|thumb|200px|A cylinder's lateral surface unrolls into a rectangle]]
For a '''[[Cylinder (geometry)|right circular cylinder]]''' with radius {{mvar|r}} and height {{mvar|h}}, the lateral surface is the curved surface connecting the two circular bases. When this surface is "unrolled" (i.e. developed into a plane), it forms a [[rectangle]] with width equal to the [[circumference]] of the base ({{math|2π''r''}}) and height {{mvar|h}}.<ref name="Alexander"/> Thus:

:{{math|1=''A''<sub>lateral</sub> = 2π''rh''}}

The total surface area of the cylinder is obtained by adding the areas of the two circular bases:

:{{math|1=''A''<sub>total</sub> = 2π''rh'' + 2π''r''<sup>2</sup> = 2π''r''(''h'' + ''r'')}}

===Pyramid===
For a [[pyramid (geometry)|pyramid]], the lateral surface area is the sum of the areas of all the triangular lateral faces, excluding the base.<ref name="Jacobs"/>

For a '''regular pyramid''' — one whose base is a [[regular polygon]] and whose apex lies directly above the centre of the base — the lateral faces are [[Congruence (geometry)|congruent]] [[isosceles triangle]]s. In this case, the lateral surface area is:<ref name="Alexander"/>

:{{math|1=''A''<sub>lateral</sub> = {{sfrac|1|2}} ''P'' ⋅ ''l''}}

where {{mvar|P}} is the perimeter of the base and {{mvar|l}} is the [[slant height]] (the distance from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge, measured along a lateral face).

===Cone===
For a '''right circular [[cone]]''' with base radius {{mvar|r}} and slant height {{mvar|l}}, the lateral surface area is:<ref name="Alexander"/>

:{{math|1=''A''<sub>lateral</sub> = π''rl''}}

The slant height can be found from the radius and the (vertical) height {{mvar|h}} of the cone using the [[Pythagorean theorem]]:

:{{math|1=''l'' = {{sqrt|''r''<sup>2</sup> + ''h''<sup>2</sup>}}}}

This formula can be understood by cutting the lateral surface of the cone along a slant line from the apex to the base and unrolling it into a flat [[Circular sector|sector]] of a circle with radius {{mvar|l}} and arc length {{math|2π''r''}}.<ref name="Alexander"/>

===Frustum===
A '''[[frustum]]''' is the portion of a cone or pyramid that lies between two parallel planes cutting through it. For a right circular [[frustum of a cone|conical frustum]] with top radius {{math|''r''<sub>1</sub>}}, bottom radius {{math|''r''<sub>2</sub>}}, and slant height {{mvar|l}}, the lateral surface area is:<ref name="Alexander"/>

:{{math|1=''A''<sub>lateral</sub> = π(''r''<sub>1</sub> + ''r''<sub>2</sub>) ⋅ ''l''}}

where the slant height is given by:

:{{math|1=''l'' = {{sqrt|(''r''<sub>2</sub> − ''r''<sub>1</sub>)<sup>2</sup> + ''h''<sup>2</sup>}}}}

This generalises the cone formula (setting {{math|1=''r''<sub>1</sub> = 0}}) and can also be seen as the difference between the lateral areas of two nested cones.
